## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The Board's central claim is that the loss of Columbia had two causes of equal weight, one physical and one organisational. Its Synopsis puts it in one sentence: "We are convinced that the management practices overseeing the Space Shuttle Program were as much a cause of the accident as the foam that struck the left wing." [V] (Synopsis, p. 11). The physical cause was a piece of insulating foam that broke from the left bipod ramp of the External Tank 81.7 seconds after launch and struck the lower half of Reinforced Carbon-Carbon (RCC) panel 8 on the left wing at 81.9 seconds, opening a breach through which superheated air entered the wing during re-entry and melted its aluminium structure [AP] (Executive Summary, p. 9; Ch 3, p. 49). The organisational causes were rooted in the programme's history and culture: the compromises made to win approval for the Shuttle, years of resource constraints, fluctuating priorities and schedule pressure, the mischaracterisation of a developmental vehicle as operational, and the lack of an agreed national vision [AP] (Ch 7, p. 177).

The argument runs from the Board Statement onward against the habit of stopping at the last broken part or the nearest person. "Too often, accident investigations blame a failure only on the last step in a complex process, when a more comprehensive understanding of that process could reveal that earlier steps might be equally or even more culpable." [V] (Board Statement, p. 6). Part Two opens with the same warning: "When the determinations of the causal chain are limited to the technical flaw and individual failure, typically the actions taken to prevent a similar event in the future are also limited: fix the technical problem and replace or retrain the individual responsible. Putting these corrections in place leads to another mistake — the belief that the problem is solved." [V] (Part Two, p. 97). Its conclusion: "In our view, the NASA organizational culture had as much to do with this accident as the foam." [V] (Part Two, p. 97).

The Board's explanation of why foam was able to destroy an Orbiter after more than a hundred flights is a history of normalisation. Foam shedding violated the Shuttle's design requirements from the first flight, yet with each successful landing it was reclassified, from a safety-of-flight concern to an "in-family" anomaly to a maintenance and turnaround issue [AR] (Ch 6, pp. 121–130; Ch 8, pp. 196–197). The Board borrows the name for this pattern, the normalisation of deviance, from the sociologist Diane Vaughan's study of the Challenger launch decision, and argues that the same pattern, and the same organisational flaws that let it run, produced both Shuttle losses [BT] (Ch 6, p. 130; Ch 8, pp. 195–197). "History is not just a backdrop or a scene-setter. History is cause. History set the Columbia and Challenger accidents in motion." [V] (Ch 8, p. 195).

During the mission itself, the Board finds that engineers' concerns were defeated rather than heard. The chapter on decision-making sets engineers' worries about risk and safety against management's belief that foam could not hurt the Orbiter and the need to keep to schedule, and shows the worries losing [AP] (Ch 6, p. 121). Three requests for imagery of the wing were made and turned down, analysis was done with a tool used far outside its validated range, and engineers were asked to prove the Orbiter was unsafe rather than managers proving it was safe [AR] (Ch 6, pp. 140–172; Ch 7, p. 190). The Board does not excuse the individuals involved, but it holds that replacing them would not fix the problem: individuals "always must assume responsibility for their actions. What it does mean is that NASA's problems cannot be solved simply by retirements, resignations, or transferring personnel." [V] (Ch 8, p. 195).

The remedy the Board proposes is structural. It recommends an independent Technical Engineering Authority that owns technical requirements and all waivers to them, a Safety and Mission Assurance organisation with direct line authority and its own resources, and a Shuttle Integration Office able to integrate every element of the programme, the Orbiter included [AP] (Ch 7, p. 193; Ch 11, p. 227). It frames these as the characteristics of organisations that manage high risk well, drawn from its study of the Navy's submarine and reactor programmes and the Aerospace Corporation [AR] (Ch 7, pp. 182–184). And it insists that the Shuttle, and human space flight generally, must be understood as developmental, not operational [AP] (Ch 9, p. 208).

## Part I: How the Board framed its work (Board Statement, Executive Summary, Synopsis, Part introductions)

### The Board Statement

The Board Statement sets out the Board's view of causation in complex systems. It holds that "complex systems almost always fail in complex ways" [V] and that a narrow focus on the last step can miss earlier steps that were equally culpable (Board Statement, p. 6). The Board grouped its findings in three categories: the physical failures, the underlying weaknesses revealed in NASA's organisation and history, and other significant observations made during the investigation that were not directly tied to the accident [AP] (Board Statement, p. 6). To understand the second category it consulted experts in organisational theory and looked at how other high-risk enterprises (nuclear power, petrochemicals, nuclear weapons production, nuclear submarines, expendable launch vehicles) run reliably [AP] (Board Statement, p. 6). It closes on the risk of space flight: "space flight is still far from routine. It involves a substantial element of risk, which must be recognized, but never accepted with resignation." [V] (Board Statement, p. 6).

### The Executive Summary and Synopsis

The investigation's scale is given in the Executive Summary: a staff of more than 120, around 400 NASA engineers in support, some 30,000 documents reviewed, more than 200 formal interviews, more than 3,000 inputs from the public, and more than 25,000 people in the debris search, during which two people died in a helicopter accident [AE] (Executive Summary, p. 9). Its mandate broadened during the work to take in NASA's history, culture, politics and budget [AP] (Executive Summary, p. 9). The Summary lists the organisational causes the later chapters develop: reliance on past success as a substitute for sound engineering practice; organisational barriers that stopped critical safety information from flowing and stifled professional differences of opinion; a lack of integrated management across programme elements; and an informal chain of command and decision-making that operated outside the organisation's rules [AP] (Executive Summary, p. 9). It names the attributes the Board wants NASA to acquire: an independent technical authority, independent safety assurance with line authority, and the characteristics of a learning organisation [AP] (Executive Summary, p. 9). It separates recommendations to be met before return to flight from those for continuing to fly [AP] (Executive Summary, p. 10).

The Synopsis gives the mission frame: STS-107 was the 113th Shuttle flight and Columbia's 28th [AE] (Synopsis, p. 11). It states the Board's verdict on the flight in one line: "Mission management failed to detect weak signals that the Orbiter was in trouble and take corrective action." [V] (Synopsis, p. 11). It previews the later chapters' findings that NASA lacked effective checks and balances, an independent safety programme and the characteristics of a learning organisation, and that the changes needed would be difficult and internally resisted [AP] (Synopsis, p. 12). It also previews the Board's charge, in Chapter 9, that NASA has a history of ignoring outside recommendations or making improvements that fade over time [AP] (Synopsis, p. 12).

### The Part introductions

Part One opens with a statement that rockets fail a few percent of the time and that the nation must continue to accept the risks of exploration [AP] (Part One, p. 19). Part Two opens with the warning against stopping at "operator error" quoted in the thesis and with the claim that complex systems run by complex organisations fail in unanticipated ways [AP] (Part Two, p. 97). It quotes a nuclear physicist's description of high-risk technology as a bargain, which is paraphrased here: society accepts the benefits of a dangerous technology in return for a commitment to vigilance from those who run it; the Board is not convinced that NASA, or the Congress and Administrations that funded it, kept that bargain [BT] (Part Two, p. 97). Part Three opens by acknowledging the diligence and professionalism of NASA's people and stating that the Board's recommendations aim at safer continued exploration, not an end to it [AP] (Part Three, p. 205).

## Part II: The accident and its physical cause (Part One, Ch 1–4)

### The evolution of the Shuttle Program (Ch 1)

The Board places the accident in the programme's origins. In its view, "the Columbia accident is not a random event, but rather a product of the Space Shuttle Program's history and current management processes" [V] (Ch 1, p. 21). Political compromises in the programme's approval produced unrealistic expectations about the vehicle, and its design made it an inherently vulnerable vehicle whose safe operation exceeded NASA's organisational capabilities [AP] (Ch 1, p. 21).

The history is told in detail [AE] (Ch 1, pp. 22–25). In 1971 the Office of Management and Budget set a ceiling of about $5 billion on development. NASA claimed in 1972 that the Shuttle could be built for $5.15 billion, fly 100 missions per vehicle and cost $7.7 million a flight, figures the budget office knew rested on optimistic studies. The economic case needed the Department of Defense as a customer and about 50 flights a year; Defense's cross-range requirement drove the delta wing and a more robust thermal protection system. Solid rocket boosters were chosen because they were cheaper to develop, and no crew escape system was provided because the vehicle was believed safer. The Board's judgement: "a Shuttle designed to be all things to all people created inherently greater risks than if more realistic technical goals had been set at the start" [V] (Ch 1, p. 23). And: "the greatest compromise NASA made was not so much with any particular element of the technical design, but rather with the premise of the vehicle itself" [V] (Ch 1, p. 23), with a persistent gap between how the Shuttle was marketed and its operational reality (Ch 1, p. 23) [AP].

Testing followed the same economy [AE] (Ch 1, pp. 23–24). Elements were ground-tested separately and analytical models used to certify the integrated system; there was no unmanned orbital test flight. Columbia was flown to Kennedy in 1979 with only about 24,000 of its 30,000 tiles installed, to keep up the appearance of the schedule. The first flight, on 12 April 1981, lost 16 tiles and damaged 148. The Shuttle was declared operational in 1982, in part in hope of winning approval for a space station and in part to compete with Europe's Ariane launcher. The promised economics never arrived: turnaround took 67 days against 10 projected, and missions cost more than $140 million, about seven times the projection. Schedule pressure produced a management atmosphere that accepted less-than-specification performance because earlier flights had succeeded, a point the Board credits to Vaughan [BT] (Ch 1, p. 24).

The Challenger accident of 28 January 1986, 73 seconds into the 25th mission, is summarised from the Rogers Commission [BT] (Ch 1, pp. 24–25). The Commission found the solid rocket booster joint design poorly understood and inadequately tested, and turned its attention to management practice once it learned that the eve-of-launch debate had not reached senior managers; it recommended a redesigned joint and an independent safety office reporting to the Administrator. Return to flight took 32 months, commercial satellites were taken off the Shuttle and Defense payloads moved to expendable launchers [AE] (Ch 1, p. 25). By STS-107, more than 44 percent of Columbia's tiles and 41 of its 44 RCC panels were original [AE] (Ch 1, p. 25). The chapter ends on the vehicle's nature: "the Space Shuttle is a developmental vehicle that operates not in routine flight but in the realm of dangerous exploration" [V] (Ch 1, p. 25).

### Columbia's final flight (Ch 2)

Chapter 2 is the record of the mission and carries no findings [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 27–48). STS-107 was a 16-day science mission with more than 70 scientists' experiments, delayed 13 times over two years by payload changes, an Orbiter maintenance period that ran six months long over wiring inspections, a four-month fleet grounding for fuel-line flowliner cracks, and the reshuffling of the manifest to fly two Station missions first (Ch 2, pp. 27–28). The crew of seven had trained for thousands of hours, and the Board's review of the maintenance and processing paperwork found nothing relevant to the accident (Ch 2, pp. 29–30).

The pre-launch record includes one item that recurs in Chapter 10: at the pre-tanking Mission Management Team meeting, the plates of the External Tank attach ring were found to be below their specified strength, and the 1.4 safety factor was waived for STS-107 [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 31–32). The chapter also sets out the management structure in flight: the Mission Management Team, chaired by the Shuttle Program's integration manager and governed by NSTS 07700 Volume VIII, and the Mission Evaluation Room, through which engineering analysis reaches it [AE] (Ch 2, p. 32).

Launch came at 10:39 a.m. on 16 January 2003 [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 33–34). A wind shear near maximum dynamic pressure at about 57 seconds raised bipod loads above normal but within design. At 81.7 seconds one large and at least two small pieces of foam left the left bipod ramp, and at 81.9 seconds the large piece struck the underside of the left wing near RCC panels 5 to 9. The Board's estimate was a piece 21 to 27 inches by 12 to 18 inches, tumbling at 18 revolutions per second or more and striking at a relative speed of 625 to 840 feet per second; nobody saw the strike in real time (Ch 2, p. 34).

The Intercenter Photo Working Group found the strike on review the day after launch, and its chair asked for high-resolution imagery from the Department of Defense, the first of three distinct requests, none of which was fulfilled [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 37–38). A Debris Assessment Team used the Crater model, which the Board notes had not been designed for this kind of impact, and briefed its results to the Mission Evaluation Room on 24 January; the Mission Evaluation Room manager gave the Mission Management Team a verbal summary without data, and the Team declared the strike a turnaround issue and did not pursue imagery (Ch 2, pp. 37–38). E-mails exploring the consequences of damage circulated among engineers but generally stayed within their senders' own speciality and rank [AP] (Ch 2, p. 38).

Re-entry is reconstructed second by second [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 38–44). After the de-orbit burn and entry interface at 8:44:09 a.m. on 1 February, the first sign of trouble was a strain sensor on the left wing spar at entry interface plus 270 seconds, recorded only on the onboard recorder, not telemetered; the entry team had no concerns about the strike and treated the re-entry like any other (Ch 2, pp. 38–39). Debris shedding was seen over California, hydraulic sensors went off-scale, tyre pressures were lost, and the last telemetry came at entry interface plus 923 seconds; videos show the Orbiter breaking up at about plus 969 seconds (Ch 2, pp. 39–44).

The search that followed covered more than 2,000 square miles in Texas and Louisiana with up to 25,000 people from some 270 organisations; a helicopter crash killed a contract pilot and a Texas Forest Service searcher [AE] (Ch 2, pp. 45–47). Searchers recovered more than 84,000 pieces weighing 84,900 pounds, about 38 percent of the Orbiter's dry weight, including the onboard recorder whose 800 sensors filled a telemetry gap; the reconstruction of the left wing showed that heat first entered where the foam had struck (Ch 2, p. 47).

### Accident analysis (Ch 3)

**The External Tank and its foam (Sec 3.2).** The bipod ramp foam was hand-sprayed and shaved, and only visually inspected [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 50–53). Its geometry had been changed after the first recorded bipod loss on STS-7, and the last change came with ET-76. The Board concludes that "A combination of factors, rather than a single factor, led to the loss of the left bipod foam ramp" [V] (Ch 3, p. 52). It criticises the testing: the tank was designed in isolation in the 1970s; the programme did not follow the principle of flying what you test and testing what you fly; and the bipod and tank were never tested or instrumented in the complex flight environment, although analysis must always be verified by test or flight data [AP] (Ch 3, p. 53). Foam is variable and its failure modes poorly understood; hand-spraying leaves defects along knit lines; and no qualified non-destructive evaluation could determine the quality of a bipod ramp [AP] (Ch 3, p. 53). The Board ruled out negligence and sabotage: "Negligence on the part of NASA, Lockheed Martin, or United Space Alliance workers does not appear to have been a factor." [V] (Ch 3, p. 53). Foam loss was visible on more than 80 percent of the 79 missions with imagery, and left bipod ramp loss on nearly 10 percent of missions where it could be seen [AE] (Ch 3, p. 53). A Board member's sidebar describes his own kitchen-table experiment with BX-250 foam on a brass plate, which showed how hydrostatic pressure cracks the foam and why the absence of foam loss in a test does not prove safety [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 54–55).

Finding F3.2-1 reads: "NASA does not fully understand the mechanisms that cause foam loss on almost all flights from larger areas of foam coverage and from areas that are sculpted by hand." [V] (Ch 3, p. 55). The first recommendation of the report, R3.2-1, is to eliminate all External Tank debris shedding at the source, with emphasis on the bipod region [AP] (Ch 3, p. 55).

**The wing leading edge (Sec 3.3).** The design requirements for the RCC system were written for 100 missions and a kinetic-energy impact of 0.006 foot-pounds, and did not require it to withstand debris or ice [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 55–56). Finding F3.3-1: "The original design specifications required the RCC components to have essentially no impact resistance." [V] (Ch 3, p. 58). Finding F3.3-2: "Current inspection techniques are not adequate to assess structural integrity of the RCC components." [V] (Ch 3, p. 58). Inspections were visual and by touch; only two flown panels had ever been destructively tested; and zinc primer leached from the launch pad by rain was causing pinholes in the panels [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 56–58).

**Image and transport analyses (Sec 3.4).** The Board ran independent tests because "The widely accepted implausibility of foam causing significant damage to the wing leading edge system led the Board to conduct independent tests" [V] (Ch 3, p. 59). The foam struck at about 545 miles per hour relative to the Orbiter: the Orbiter, in the Board's phrase, "ran into" the foam as the foam decelerated [AE] (Ch 3, p. 60). The cameras that tracked the ascent were legacy equipment, one out of focus [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 60–61). A finding with consequences for Chapter 6 is that the information available during the mission was adequate to determine the strike's effect on both tiles and RCC [AP] (Ch 3, p. 62). The recommendations call for at least three useful views of every ascent, written into the Launch Commit Criteria, and for imagery of the External Tank after separation and of the wing underside on orbit [AP] (Ch 3, p. 62).

**The Flight Day 2 object (Sec 3.5).** An object departed the Orbiter on 17 January during manoeuvres and was tracked by radar until it decayed; only a fragment of RCC panel of at least 140 square inches matched its radar cross-section and ballistic coefficient [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 62–63).

**Re-entry (Sec 3.6).** The Orbiter's experimental sensor suite was 22 years old, twice its specified life, and "of the 181 sensors in Columbia's wings, 55 had already failed or were producing questionable readings before STS-107 was launched" [V] (Ch 3, p. 65). From the recovered recorder the Board reconstructs a breach of about ten inches in the lower RCC near panel 8, hot gas that burned through the wing spar by entry interface plus 487 seconds, growing heating in the wheel well, and aerodynamic changes that the flight control system fought until control was lost at about plus 970 seconds [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 64–73). Finding F3.6-5: "By the time data indicating problems was telemetered to Mission Control Center, the Orbiter had already suffered damage from which it could not recover." [V] (Ch 3, p. 73).

**Debris analysis (Sec 3.7).** Forensic work on the recovered debris independently located the breach: slag deposits, rib erosion and the debris field's geography all point to the lower part of RCC panel 8-left [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 73–77). A sidebar on crew survivability records that the crew module broke apart over about 24 seconds, that the crew died of blunt trauma and hypoxia, and that the moment of death cannot be determined [AE] (Ch 3, p. 77).

**Impact testing (Sec 3.8).** The Board took a direct role in testing because of the continuing debate over the projectile's size, "largely due to the Marshall Space Flight Center's insistence that, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, the foam could have been no larger than 855 cubic inches" [V], and because NASA kept relying on Crater, a semi-empirical model built from Apollo-era data [AP] (Ch 3, p. 78). The aim was to "prove or disprove the impression that foam could not break an RCC panel" [V] (Ch 3, p. 78). At the Southwest Research Institute, a 1.67-pound foam block fired at 777 feet per second into a flown RCC panel 8 from Atlantis opened a hole of about 16 by 17 inches [AE] (Ch 3, pp. 81–83). "The test clearly demonstrated that a foam impact of the type Columbia sustained could seriously breach the Wing Leading Edge Structural Subsystem." [V] (Ch 3, p. 83). The tests, the Board says, also "counteracted the lingering denial or discounting of the analytic evidence" [V] (Ch 3, p. 83). Finding F3.8-6: "NASA's current tools, including the Crater model, are inadequate to evaluate Orbiter Thermal Protection System damage from debris impacts during pre-launch, on-orbit, and post-launch activity." [V] (Ch 3, p. 83). The recommendations ask for spare RCC panels sufficient to free maintenance decisions from schedule and cost pressure, and for physics-based damage models with damage thresholds that trigger on-orbit inspection and repair [AP] (Ch 3, p. 84).

### Other factors considered (Ch 4)

A fault tree of more than 3,000 elements, worked by six component teams and a systems-integration team, closed out most alternative explanations [AE] (Ch 4, pp. 85–86). The chapter still records lapses found along the way [AE] (Ch 4, pp. 86–96). Bolt catchers had been qualified by "analysis and similarity" on 24-year-old tests of a different design; every unit tested failed below its expected load, and the Board attributes the lapse to inadequate oversight and confusion over the requirement among NASA, United Space Alliance and the Defense Contract Management Agency (Ch 4, pp. 86–87). Kapton wiring, a crushed piece of foam under the left bipod strut after the tank was de-mated in a manifest reshuffle, space weather, a 1999 hydraulic spill, wing roughness, flight-controller training, payloads and willful damage were all examined and ruled out (Ch 4, pp. 88–93). Two Michoud closeouts were done by a single person, prompting a recommendation that at least two employees attend every final closeout [AP] (Ch 4, p. 93). The micrometeoroid and orbital-debris risk was estimated at about 1 in 370 for STS-107 and 1 in 3 cumulatively over the programme: "The Board considers this probability of a critical penetration to be unacceptably high." [V] (Ch 4, p. 94). At Kennedy, a 2001 change had split "foreign object damage" into "processing debris" and "foreign object debris", a split the Board calls statistically deceptive, recommending a return to the industry-standard definition [AP] (Ch 4, p. 95).

## Part III: Why the accident occurred (Part Two, Ch 5–8)

### From Challenger to Columbia (Ch 5)

Chapter 5 traces the policy and budget environment between the two accidents [AR] (Ch 5, pp. 99–118). After the Cold War, the programme lost the competition that had underpinned it, yet NASA kept an ambitious agenda; the drive for efficiency meant downsizing, outsourcing (including safety oversight) and the consideration of privatisation [AP] (Ch 5, p. 99). The Board sees "unfortunate similarities between the agency's performance and safety practices in both periods" [V] (Ch 5, p. 99).

**Post-Challenger reform, partly undone.** The Rogers Commission's findings and recommendations are summarised, not quoted, here [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 99–100): the joint and seal failure, missed warning signs as joint anomalies came to be accepted as flight risk, a silent safety system, and schedule pressure that compressed training and drained spare parts. After return to flight, an Office of Safety, Reliability and Quality Assurance was created at headquarters but without the direct authority the Commission intended, and the Centers kept their own safety organisations reporting to Center Directors [AE] (Ch 5, p. 101). The Space Station became the primary driver of the Shuttle's launch schedule [AP] (Ch 5, p. 101). The Board's summary of where things stood by 2003: "By the eve of the Columbia accident, institutional practices that were in effect at the time of the Challenger accident — such as inadequate concern over deviations from expected performance, a silent safety program, and schedule pressure — had returned to NASA." [V] (Ch 5, p. 101).

**Human space flight culture.** The chapter's sidebar defines organisational culture in everyday terms as the way things are done in a place [AP] (Ch 5, p. 101). The Apollo-era culture is described as a "can-do" culture that accepted risk and failure as part of the work while valuing rigorous attention to detail [AP] (Ch 5, pp. 101–102). Drawing on outside observers, the Board describes an agency that saw itself as beyond reproach, lost the ability to take criticism and rejected the recommendations of many advisory bodies, the Rogers Commission among them [BT] (Ch 5, p. 102). Its own judgement: "the Board views this cultural resistance as a fundamental impediment to NASA's effective organizational performance" [V] (Ch 5, p. 102).

**Too much with too little.** NASA's share of the federal budget fell from about 4 percent in the Apollo years to 1 percent or less from the 1970s on; between 1993 and 2002 NASA lost 13 percent of its purchasing power while discretionary spending rose 25 percent [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 102–103). The Shuttle was hit hardest: its budget fell from $4.128 billion in FY1993 to $2.977 billion in FY1998, and Station overruns had to be absorbed within the human space flight budget, so the programme lost about 40 percent of its purchasing power over the decade [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 104–105). Upgrades and infrastructure were deferred while the costs of an ageing system rose [AP] (Ch 5, p. 105).

**Turbulence.** The 1990s brought a torrent of management change under Administrator Daniel Goldin, including business principles that treated checks and balances as unnecessary and placed responsibility for quality on workers [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 105–106). "It is arguable whether these business principles can readily be applied to a government agency operating under civil service rules and in a politicized environment." [V] (Ch 5, p. 106). The Shuttle workforce was the main target of savings: between 1991 and 1994 operating costs fell 21 percent, contractor staff from 28,394 to 22,387 and NASA staff from 4,031 to 2,959, and a 1995 review cut a further 5,900 positions on the assurance that safety would not be compromised [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 107–108). In 1996 Johnson was again made lead center, restoring the pre-Challenger structure; NASA's top safety official objected that it was a safety issue and resigned [AE] (Ch 5, p. 107).

**The Space Flight Operations Contract.** The 1995 Kraft Report described the Shuttle as a mature and reliable system and recommended reducing safety and quality-assurance oversight; the Board judges that "The report characterized the Space Shuttle in a way that the Board judges to be at odds with the realities of the Shuttle Program" [V] (Ch 5, p. 108). Critics at the time, including the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel and a senior engineer who wrote to the President, warned that removing checks and balances endangered the programme; their words are paraphrased here [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 108–109). United Space Alliance, a 50–50 venture of Lockheed Martin and Rockwell, took on safety, inspection and integration tasks that NASA had held, while NASA kept the management of the overall process of ensuring Shuttle safety [AE] (Ch 5, p. 109). By the end of the decade, Shuttle civil-service staffing had fallen sharply at every Center; "By the end of the decade, NASA realized that staff reductions had gone too far." [V] (Ch 5, p. 110).

**When to replace the Shuttle.** Policy wavered between ending the programme soon and flying it for decades, which produced "limited and inconsistent investments" [V] in upgrades and infrastructure (Ch 5, p. 110). Successor programmes were cancelled one after another (the National Aerospace Plane, X-33, X-34, the Space Launch Initiative), and the planned replacement date "was consistent only in its inconsistency: it changed from 2002 to 2006 to 2012, and before the Columbia accident, to 2020 or later" [V] (Ch 5, p. 111). Safety upgrades were cut, among them a 34 percent cut to the five-year safety-upgrade budget in FY2003 as operating costs rose, and infrastructure decayed to the point that nets were hung in the Vehicle Assembly Building to catch falling concrete [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 114–115).

**The return of schedule pressure.** When the Space Station ran $4 billion over budget in 2001, NASA committed to a "U.S. Core Complete" milestone with Node 2 to be launched on 19 February 2004, and the Station's progress was subjected to a performance gate [AE] (Ch 5, pp. 116–117). "The White House and Congress had put the International Space Station Program, the Space Shuttle Program, and indeed NASA on probation." [V] (Ch 5, p. 117). NASA management treated an on-schedule Node 2 launch as the test of its credibility. "Any suggestions that it would be difficult to meet that launch date were brushed aside." [V] and "This insistence on a fixed launch schedule was worrisome." [V] (Ch 5, p. 117). Even non-Station missions such as STS-107 were tied to the date, because Columbia was to be modified for Station flights after its return [AE] (Ch 5, p. 117).

**Conclusion.** The Board names three factors: a budget and workforce cut by more than 40 percent; the characterisation of the Shuttle as mature and reliable, which led NASA to reduce its direct involvement in safety and to monitor its contractor from a distance; and the shifting replacement date that deferred upgrades and infrastructure [AR] (Ch 5, pp. 117–118). "The Board observes that this is hardly an environment in which those responsible for safe operation of the Shuttle can function without being influenced by external pressures." [V] (Ch 5, p. 118). "The Program was operating too close to too many margins." [V] (Ch 5, p. 118). The Board found no evidence that contract consolidation itself added technical risk, but it complicated an already complex structure and created barriers to communication [AP] (Ch 5, p. 118).

### Decision making at NASA (Ch 6)

The chapter has four sections: the history of foam anomalies, schedule pressure, the decisions made during STS-107, and the possibility of rescue or repair [AP] (Ch 6, p. 121). It opens by saying that turbulence in the programme (complexity, shifting authority, ambiguous relationships) "repeatedly influenced decisions made before and during STS-107" [V] (Ch 6, p. 121), and that a latent assumption ran through the mission: that even if the damage had been found, nothing could have been done [AP] (Ch 6, p. 121).

#### A history of foam anomalies (Sec 6.1)

"Damage caused by debris has occurred on every Space Shuttle flight, and most missions have had insulating foam shed during ascent." [V] (Ch 6, p. 121). The Shuttle's own design requirements prohibited debris shedding that could damage the Orbiter and set an impact limit of 0.006 foot-pounds; the Thermal Protection System is so fragile that a thumbnail can mark a tile [AE] (Ch 6, p. 121). Foam shedding was seen on 65 of 79 missions with imagery; the Orbiter averaged 143 debris hits a mission, 31 of them larger than an inch, and the Board concludes that foam is likely responsible for most of them [AE] (Ch 6, p. 122).

The Board describes how the meaning of foam shedding shifted. "With each successful landing, it appears that NASA engineers and managers increasingly regarded the foam-shedding as inevitable, and as either unlikely to jeopardize safety or simply an acceptable risk." [V] (Ch 6, p. 122). A sidebar quotes NASA's own definitions of "in family", "out of family", "accepted risk" and "no safety-of-flight issue" [AE] (Ch 6, p. 122). The left bipod ramp shed foam on seven of 113 missions (about 10 percent of those imaged), while the right never did, and "NASA could not explain why only the left bipod experienced foam loss" [V] (Ch 6, p. 123).

The Board walks through each bipod event [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 123–126). After STS-7 (1983), the first, the anomaly was closed on the basis of Orbiter repairs without reference to fixing the cause of the shedding. After STS-32R (1990), the Board notes "the persistent uncertainty about the causes of foam loss and potential Orbiter damage results from a lack of thorough hazard analysis and engineering attention" [V] (Ch 6, p. 124). After STS-50 (1992), which caused the largest tile damage in the programme's history, one office closed the anomaly as an "accepted flight risk" and another as "not a safety of flight issue", two different categories (Ch 6, p. 124). Two further events, STS-52 and STS-62, were found only after the accident, when the Board ordered a review of the film (Ch 6, p. 124). A sidebar explains why five of the seven known events were on Columbia: its umbilical-well cameras had imaged the tank on 26 of 28 missions, a sample bias rather than a property of Columbia [AE] (Ch 6, p. 123).

**STS-112 and the STS-113 Flight Readiness Review.** On STS-112 in October 2002, a piece of bipod foam about 4 by 5 by 12 inches struck the booster's External Tank attach ring [AE] (Ch 6, p. 124). The Board counts the decisions that followed among those "most directly linked to the STS-107 accident" [AP] (Ch 6, p. 125). The Intercenter Photo Working Group recommended an In-Flight Anomaly; the Program Requirements Control Board instead assigned the External Tank Project an "action", inconsistent with prior practice, due after the next launch and then slipped until after STS-107 [AE] (Ch 6, p. 125). "The Space Shuttle Program decided to fly not one but two missions before resolving the STS-112 foam loss." [V] (Ch 6, p. 125). The Board explains why managers were content: over time they had been conditioned not to see foam loss or debris as a safety-of-flight concern, and the Node 2 schedule and the Station crew's 180-day limit pressed on the decision [AP] (Ch 6, p. 125).

The flight rationale briefed at the STS-113 Flight Readiness Review is reproduced and judged. "This rationale is seriously flawed." [V] (Ch 6, p. 126). Its statements about the design were incorrect, its probability argument could equally have said the risk was as high as before, and "With no engineering analysis, Shuttle managers used past success as a justification for future flights" [V] (Ch 6, p. 126). A headquarters safety estimate of 99 percent probability that the bipod would not shed is dismissed as an effort to make the risk look low rather than a serious grappling with it [AP] (Ch 6, p. 126). The terms "accepted risk" and "no safety-of-flight issue" became blurred, the hazard report for debris was never updated, and "no process addresses the need to update a hazard analysis when anomalies occur" [V] (Ch 6, p. 126). The rationale "cleared the way for Columbia's launch and provided a method for Mission managers to classify the STS-107 foam strike as a maintenance and turnaround concern" [V] (Ch 6, p. 126). The STS-107 Flight Readiness Review never discussed the STS-112 loss at all [AE] (Ch 6, p. 126).

**STS-27R and institutional memory.** The largest earlier debris event, on Atlantis in 1988, damaged 707 tiles and nearly burned through; that crew inspected the Orbiter with the robot arm [AE] (Ch 6, p. 127). The Board sets this against STS-107, where inspection and imaging were declined: "The Board views the failure to do so as an illustration of the lack of institutional memory in the Space Shuttle Program that supports the Board's claim, discussed in Chapter 7, that NASA is not functioning as a learning organization." [V] (Ch 6, p. 127). A table of 14 debris events shows the drift [AE] (Ch 6, p. 128). STS-35 was the first time foam was called both a safety-of-flight issue and a turnaround issue. After STS-42 the next flight launched without the debris anomaly closed. STS-56 and STS-58 were dispositioned as "in family", which the Board says demonstrates "the increasingly casual ways in which debris impacts were dispositioned" [V] (Ch 6, p. 128). STS-87 (1997), with 308 hits, was traced to a change in the foam's blowing agent, and the fixes merely brought shedding back to earlier levels (Ch 6, p. 128). A 1990 probabilistic study that put tile-loss risk at about 1 in 1,000 a mission, with debris as 40 percent of it, had not been fully used [BT] (Ch 6, pp. 129–130).

**Conclusion.** "Over the course of 113 missions, foam-shedding and other debris impacts came to be regarded more as a turnaround or maintenance issue, and less as a hazard to the vehicle and crew." [V] (Ch 6, p. 130). Managers appear to have confused "accepted risk" with "not a safety-of-flight issue", schedule pressure appears to have cut engineering work short, and hazard analyses neither succeeded nor were adjusted [AP] (Ch 6, p. 130). The Board names the pattern as the "normalization of deviance" described by Vaughan, and paraphrases a comparison from Feynman's appendix to the Rogers report [BT] (Ch 6, p. 130). Finding F6.1-1: "NASA has not followed its own rules and requirements on foam-shedding. Although the agency continuously worked on the foam-shedding problem, the debris impact requirements have not been met on any mission." [V] (Ch 6, p. 130). Finding F6.1-4: "There is lack of effective processes for feedback or integration among project elements in the resolution of In-Flight Anomalies." [V] (Ch 6, p. 131). Finding F6.1-10: "NASA failed to adequately perform trend analysis on foam losses. This greatly hampered the agency's ability to make informed decisions about foam losses." [V] (Ch 6, p. 131).

#### Schedule pressure (Sec 6.2)

During interviews, NASA staff raised the 19 February 2004 Node 2 date without being asked [AE] (Ch 6, p. 131). The Board's view of aggressive schedules is balanced: "Aggressive schedules by themselves are often a sign of a healthy institution." [V] (Ch 6, p. 131). But upper management said there was no undue pressure while the workforce described a heavy focus on the date and safety concerns, and "The weight of evidence supports the workforce view." [V] (Ch 6, p. 131). Monthly briefings to the Administrator gave more than half their slides to Node 2 margin; managers worked holidays, cut testing at Kennedy, ran tasks in parallel and added a third shift; "Days of margin in that schedule were one of the principle metrics by which both programs came to be judged." [V] (Ch 6, p. 132). A screen saver counting down to the date was distributed; employees found it amusing because they knew the date could not be met, but it carried the message all the same [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 132–133).

The Core Complete date had been realistic when approved, but the serial Station manifest left the Shuttle "under the gun", and when the fleet was grounded in mid-2002 and Columbia was slated for Station flights after STS-107, "This decision put Columbia directly in the path of Core Complete." [V] (Ch 6, p. 134). Every bit of padding was gone by December 2002; four Station launches were planned in five months, a rate comparable to the pre-Challenger tempo the Rogers Commission had criticised, and the processing schedule had no margin for any slip [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 135–137). Seven flight controllers were flying without current certification because recertification had been deferred under schedule pressure [AE] (Ch 6, p. 137).

The Board describes a "can-do" attitude in which people were praised for finding margin and found it hard to admit that something could not or should not be done [AP] (Ch 6, p. 138). "No one at NASA wants to be the one to stand up and say, "We can't make that date."" [V] (Ch 6, p. 138). The Mission Management Team chair was also the launch integration manager for the next flight, and the Board finds that most of her foam inquiries during the mission concerned STS-114 rather than Columbia: "most of the Shuttle Program's concern about Columbia's foam strike were not about the threat it might pose to the vehicle in orbit, but about the threat it might pose to the schedule" [V] (Ch 6, p. 139). The commitment to the date, in the Board's view, may well have subtly influenced how managers handled both the STS-112 and STS-107 strikes [AP] (Ch 6, p. 139). Finding F6.2-5: "There was no schedule margin to accommodate unforeseen problems. When flights come in rapid succession, there is no assurance that anomalies on one flight will be identified and appropriately addressed before the next flight." [V] (Ch 6, p. 139). The chapter's sidebar on risk states the mechanism: "When a program agrees to spend less money or accelerate a schedule beyond what the engineers and program managers think is reasonable, a small amount of overall risk is added." [V] (Ch 6, p. 139), and "Little by little, NASA was accepting more and more risk in order to stay on schedule." [V] (Ch 6, p. 139). Recommendation R6.2-1 asks for a flight schedule consistent with available resources, with deadlines regularly evaluated so that any added risk is recognised, understood and acceptable [AP] (Ch 6, p. 139).

#### Decision-making during the flight of STS-107 (Sec 6.3)

The section reconstructs the mission day by day from e-mails, logs, meeting transcripts and interviews [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 140–170). The named individuals' own words in those records are paraphrased here.

**Discovery and the first request (Flight Day 2).** The Intercenter Photo Working Group found the strike on 17 January. Of the tracking cameras, none had a clear view: one lost track, one was out of focus because of a badly maintained lens, and one saw only the upper side (Ch 6, p. 140). "NASA's ability to track ascending Shuttles has atrophied — a development that reflects NASA's disregard of the developmental nature of the Shuttle's technology" [V] (Ch 6, p. 140). The working group's chair asked for imagery, the first of three discrete requests; the Board also counts at least eight "missed opportunities" [AE] (Ch 6, p. 140).

**An early mindset.** Early e-mailed opinions that RCC was resilient may have contributed to a mindset that foam hitting RCC was not a concern [AP] (Ch 6, p. 141). Because the strike was out of family, a Mission Evaluation Room Tiger Team should have been formed; instead a Debris Assessment Team was set up that Program managers did not own, leaving it in organisational limbo with only a 24 January deadline [AP] (Ch 6, p. 142). Concern differed by group: the photo group believed there was damage while some managers did not, and before any analysis had started, Shuttle Program managers officially shared their belief that the strike posed no safety issue [AP] (Ch 6, p. 142). The co-chairs classified the strike as out of family [AE] (Ch 6, p. 142).

**The analysis (Flight Days 3–4).** Boeing analysts worked through the weekend; their estimates of the debris size and speed were, in the Board's words, "remarkably accurate" [AE] (Ch 6, p. 143). But the Crater model they used was calibrated for projectiles of about 3 cubic inches, and the debris was estimated at up to 640 times larger (the Board's best estimate is 400 times); this "compromised NASA's ability to accurately predict debris damage in ways that Debris Assessment Team engineers did not fully comprehend" [V] (Ch 6, p. 143). A sidebar on Crater explains that it was conservative within its limits, but "When used outside its validated limits, Crater's precision is unknown." [V] (Ch 6, p. 144). The engineer running it had used it only twice before, the work had recently moved from Huntington Beach to Houston, and when Crater predicted penetration beyond the tile depth the result was discounted as conservative [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 144–145). For RCC, only one of 15 trajectory scenarios struck RCC, and the conclusion of no penetration rested on extrapolation that made some engineers uncomfortable; "The assumptions and uncertainty embedded in this analysis were never fully presented to the Mission Evaluation Room or the Mission Management Team." [V] (Ch 6, p. 145). An e-mail asking whether the crew could inspect the wing went unanswered (Missed Opportunity 1) [AE] (Ch 6, p. 145).

**Classifying the strike as familiar (Flight Days 5–6).** A Mission Evaluation Room log compared the debris to that seen on STS-112, which the Board calls an initial attempt by managers to classify the strike as close to the experience base, without examining that the impact sites differed [AP] (Ch 6, p. 146). The Mission Management Team met only five times during the 16-day mission, although its rules called for daily meetings [AE] (Ch 6, p. 147). At its 21 January meeting the chair indicated that there was not much to be done about it in flight; in e-mails the same day she and the programme manager called the STS-113 rationale poor, and the Board finds that her attention "had already shifted from the threat the foam posed to STS-107 to the downstream implications" [AP] (Ch 6, pp. 147–148). Nobody asked the crew whether they had filmed the tank at separation (Missed Opportunity 2) [AE] (Ch 6, p. 148).

**Informal channels (Flight Days 6–7).** A flight director's log entry showed that the Mission Operations Directorate was, in the Board's words, part of "an informal chain of command, in which the Mission Operations Directorate figures prominently" [AP] (Ch 6, p. 149). A trusted thermal-protection expert, a tile specialist rather than an RCC specialist, advised early that the strike should not be a problem, and "the bounds of Schomburg's expertise were never properly qualified or questioned" [V] (Ch 6, p. 149). The previously accepted STS-113 rationale gave managers and engineers a strong incentive to use the same judgement again, since arguing otherwise would contradict an established consensus [AP] (Ch 6, p. 150). A second imagery request travelled from a Johnson manager through a Kennedy manager to the Defense Department's Shuttle support office [AE] (Ch 6, p. 150). The Debris Assessment Team's own request, the third, went through the Engineering Directorate because the Mission Management Team and Mission Evaluation Room managers were not taking part, and "Routing the request through the Engineering department led in part to it being viewed by Shuttle Program managers as a non-critical engineering desire rather than a critical operational need." [V] (Ch 6, p. 152).

**The requests cancelled (Flight Day 7).** On 22 January the three requests were dismissed, and the Debris Assessment Team took the halt as a final denial [AE] (Ch 6, p. 152). A Kennedy manager had phoned a Defense representative without the chair's authorisation, and Strategic Command had begun planning (Missed Opportunity 4); two safety officials, one of them NASA's most senior, were contacted and deferred to programme management (Missed Opportunities 5 and 6). "Despite two safety officials being contacted, one of whom was NASA's highest-ranking safety official, safety personnel took no actions to obtain imagery." [V] (Ch 6, p. 153). The request was "both made and rescinded within 90 minutes" [V] (Ch 6, p. 153). The chair asked whether anyone had a "requirement" for imagery and found none, but "she never asked them directly if the request was theirs, even though they were the team analyzing the foam strike" [V] (Ch 6, p. 153). No one in the operational chain held the clearances needed to know what national imaging assets could do, so "members of the Mission Management Team were making critical decisions about imagery capabilities based on little or no knowledge" [V] (Ch 6, p. 154).

**The right question, no follow-through.** E-mails among managers acknowledged that the programme had concluded it could not rule out catastrophic debris damage and named RCC among the critical areas [AE] (Ch 6, p. 155). The Board: "Here, all the key managers were asking the right question and admitting the danger. They even identified RCC as a critical impact zone." [V] (Ch 6, p. 156). Yet little follow-through occurred on either the imagery or the analysis [AP] (Ch 6, p. 156).

**The "mandatory need".** The Debris Assessment Team put a "need/rationale for mandatory viewing" on its agenda, and its second meeting met the phrase with shrugs [AE] (Ch 6, p. 156). The engineers were in the "unenviable position of wanting images to more accurately assess damage while simultaneously needing to prove to Program managers, as a result of their assessment, that there was a need for images in the first place" [V] (Ch 6, p. 157). The team's co-chair drafted an e-mail pressing for imagery and did not send it, because he did not want to jump the chain of command [AE] (Ch 6, p. 157). On Flight Day 8 an e-mail to the crew from Mission Control said there was no concern for RCC or tile damage and none for entry, sent because the crew might be asked about the strike at a press event [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 158–159). At the team's third meeting no alternate trajectory was considered and the imaging slide was dropped [AE] (Ch 6, p. 160).

**The briefing (Flight Day 9).** The Debris Assessment Team briefed a standing-room-only Mission Evaluation Room on five scenarios, all concerning tile rather than RCC, and named the uncertainties [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 160–161). Management "focused on the answer" rather than on the uncertainties [AP] (Ch 6, p. 160). At the Mission Management Team, the briefing became a short verbal summary without charts, and "no supporting analysis or examination of minority engineering views was asked for or offered" [AP] (Ch 6, p. 161). The meeting's minutes omitted the strike [AE] (Ch 6, p. 162). In later days the engineers still wanted images but had given up trying to make that wish fit the "mandatory" requirement [AE] (Ch 6, p. 163). Langley and Ames engineers ran simulations of landing with flat tyres after hours and circulated their results widely, but were reticent to notify the Mission Management Team [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 164–165). Imagery was offered on a not-to-interfere basis on 29 January, and none was taken [AE] (Ch 6, p. 166).

**The Board's analysis of the mission's decisions.** The Board traces the failures to several roots [AR] (Ch 6, pp. 166–170):

- *Flawed analysis.* An inexperienced team used a tool outside its range. "Engineering solutions presented to management should have included a quantifiable range of uncertainty and risk analysis" [V] (Ch 6, p. 168).
- *Management's low concern.* Managers had become inured to foam losses and believed RCC was impervious [AP] (Ch 6, p. 169). "The engineers found themselves in the unusual position of having to prove that the situation was unsafe — a reversal of the usual requirement to prove that a situation is safe." [V] (Ch 6, p. 169). An early expert opinion reinforced what managers already thought: "Mission management welcomed this opinion and sought no others." [V] (Ch 6, p. 169).
- *An unofficial hierarchy.* Debris Assessment Team members feared being ridiculed if they pressed [AP] (Ch 6, p. 169).
- *Lack of clear communication.* "Managers' tendency to accept opinions that agree with their own dams the flow of effective communications." [V] (Ch 6, p. 169). Engineers had an obligation to make their concerns heard, but leaders had a corresponding and perhaps greater obligation to create viable routes for them, and a cultural fence stood between engineers and managers [AP] (Ch 6, p. 169).
- *Lack of effective leadership.* "Managers' claims that they didn't hear the engineers' concerns were due in part to their not asking or listening." [V] (Ch 6, p. 170).
- *The failure of safety's role.* Safety personnel were present but passive [AP] (Ch 6, p. 170).

The Board's summary is that management showed no interest in understanding a problem and its implications, and that its blind spots came from the organisation [AP] (Ch 6, p. 170). It warns against reading the account as a story of bad individuals: replacing the people would not solve the problem, because people's actions are shaped by the organisations in which they work [AP] (Ch 6, p. 170).

**Findings.** Among the section's findings, numbered to F6.3-29 (several numbers are lost in conversion) [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 170–172): the Debris Assessment Team was not designated a Tiger Team and no Mission manager appeared to "own" its actions; routing its request through the Engineering Directorate diluted its urgency; the Crater simulation was well outside its test database and RCC conclusions rested on judgement rather than analysis; the assumptions and uncertainties of the analysis were never presented or discussed in full to the Mission Evaluation Room or the Mission Management Team; the briefings did not address RCC and no manager asked about it; the Mission Management Team met five times, not daily; managers entered the mission believing, from the STS-113 review, that foam was not a safety-of-flight issue. F6.3-18: "After Program managers learned about the foam strike, their belief that it would not be a problem was confirmed (early, and without analysis) by a trusted expert who was readily accessible and spoke from "experience." No one in management questioned this conclusion." [V] (Ch 6, p. 172). F6.3-19: "Managers asked "Who's requesting the photos?" instead of assessing the merits of the request." [V] (Ch 6, p. 172). F6.3-22 records that engineers had to produce evidence that the system was unsafe rather than prove it safe [AP] (Ch 6, p. 172). F6.3-23: "the focus was on the bottom line — was there a safety-of-flight issue, or not? There was little discussion of analysis, assumptions, issues, or ramifications." [V] (Ch 6, p. 172). F6.3-24: "Communication did not flow effectively up to or down from Program managers." [V] (Ch 6, p. 172). F6.3-28: "Communication was stifled by the Shuttle Program attempts to find out who had a "mandatory requirement" for imagery." [V] (Ch 6, p. 172). F6.3-29 finds that safety representatives attended every relevant meeting but were passive, and so were not a channel for concerns or dissent [AP] (Ch 6, p. 172). Recommendation R6.3-1 asks for Mission Management Team training on crew and vehicle contingencies beyond launch and ascent, full of uncertainties and unknowns and requiring the team to work across NASA and contractor lines; R6.3-2 asks for on-orbit imaging of every flight as a standard requirement [AP] (Ch 6, p. 172).

#### Rescue or repair (Sec 6.4)

At the Board's request, NASA studied whether the crew could have been saved had the damage been found by Flight Day 5 [AE] (Ch 6, pp. 173–174). Carbon-dioxide scrubbing limited the stay to Flight Day 30 (15 February). An on-orbit repair, packing an assumed six-inch hole with metal and a bag of water frozen to ice, was rated "high risk". A rescue by Atlantis, readied around the clock without skipping testing, could have launched on 10 February, leaving a five-day window. "This rescue was considered challenging but feasible." [V] (Ch 6, p. 174). It needed problem-free processing and a flawless countdown, and was conceivable only if managers had grasped the threat and determined before Flight Day 7 that there was potentially catastrophic damage [AP] (Ch 6, p. 174). Recommendation R6.4-1 asks for a practicable capability to inspect and repair Thermal Protection System damage on orbit [AP] (Ch 6, p. 174).

### The accident's organisational causes (Ch 7)

The chapter opens with the Board's critique of how investigations usually reason. "Many accident investigations make the same mistake in defining causes. They identify the widget that broke or malfunctioned, then locate the person most closely connected with the technical failure" [V] (Ch 7, p. 177). The result is a correction that fixes the part and replaces or retrains the person: "Such corrections lead to a misguided and potentially disastrous belief that the underlying problem has been solved." [V] (Ch 7, p. 177).

**The organisational cause statement.** The Board's formal statement is quoted in full because it is the report's organising claim: "The organizational causes of this accident are rooted in the Space Shuttle Program's history and culture, including the original compromises that were required to gain approval for the Shuttle Program, subsequent years of resource constraints, fluctuating priorities, schedule pressures, mischaracterizations of the Shuttle as operational rather than developmental, and lack of an agreed national vision. Cultural traits and organizational practices detrimental to safety and reliability were allowed to develop, including: reliance on past success as a substitute for sound engineering practices (such as testing to understand why systems were not performing in accordance with requirements/specifications); organizational barriers which prevented effective communication of critical safety information and stifled professional differences of opinion; lack of integrated management across program elements; and the evolution of an informal chain of command and decision-making processes that operated outside the organization's rules." [V] (Ch 7, p. 177).

**Understanding causes.** "In the Board's view, NASA's organizational culture and structure had as much to do with this accident as the External Tank foam." [V] (Ch 7, p. 177). Culture is defined as "the values, norms, beliefs, and practices that govern how an institution functions" [V], a force that "can persist through reorganizations and the reassignment of key personnel" [V] (Ch 7, p. 177). The managers' attitudes were "clearly overconfident and often bureaucratic in nature. They deferred to layered and cumbersome regulations rather than the fundamentals of safety." [V] (Ch 7, p. 177). The Board expected to find a vigorous safety organisation; NASA's briefings described a culture in which anyone could stop an operation at the first sign of a problem, but "Unfortunately, NASA's views of its safety culture in those briefings did not reflect reality." [V] (Ch 7, p. 177). Safety personnel had accepted critical risks without qualitative or quantitative support [AP] (Ch 7, p. 177). "A pattern of acceptance prevailed throughout the organization that tolerated foam problems without sufficient engineering justification for doing so." [V] (Ch 7, p. 178).

**Insights from history (Sec 7.1).** The Board traces NASA's safety organisation from a decentralised loose federation of contractor and project-office oversight in the 1960s, through the creation of the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel after the Apollo 1 fire, to the post-Challenger headquarters safety office that lacked direct authority and depended on programme funding [AE] (Ch 7, pp. 178–179). A 1990 General Accounting Office report found that NASA lacked an independent and effective safety organisation and recommended centralised funding; NASA did not adopt it, and "The problems outlined in 1990 persist to this day." [V] (Ch 7, p. 179). The 1996 Space Flight Operations Contract moved experienced engineers, increased dependence on contractors and placed less experienced engineers in management roles; collectively this "eroded NASA's in-house engineering and technical capabilities" [V] and, with the rollback of tens of thousands of government inspection points, "rendered NASA's already problematic safety system simultaneously weaker and more complex" [V] (Ch 7, p. 179). The Shuttle Independent Assessment Team (1999), the NASA Integrated Action Team (2000) and the 2002 Competitive Sourcing Task Force all reported the same communication and independence problems the Rogers Commission had found; their words are paraphrased here [BT] (Ch 7, pp. 179–180). The Board agrees with the task force that an independent safety function must be able to stop a launch or intervene after launch [AP] (Ch 7, p. 180).

**Insights from theory (Sec 7.2).** The Board consulted experts in High Reliability Theory, Normal Accident Theory and organisational theory, and held a forum on the elements of a sound safety programme [BT] (Ch 7, p. 180). It summarises the two theories as it uses them: High Reliability Theory holds that well-designed and well-managed organisations can compensate for human shortcomings; Normal Accident Theory holds that organisational and technological complexity makes failure inevitable [BT] (Ch 7, p. 180). Neither fits the accident fully, but the Board draws motifs from both [AR] (Ch 7, pp. 180–181):

- *Commitment to a safety culture.* "NASA's safety culture has become reactive, complacent, and dominated by unjustified optimism." [V] Checks and balances eroded "in favor of detailed processes that produce massive amounts of data and unwarranted consensus, but little effective communication" [V] (Ch 7, p. 180).
- *Operating centralised and decentralised.* The ability to do both as appropriate is the hallmark of a high-reliability organisation. The Debris Assessment Team was well led and had the right expertise, but its charter was "fuzzy" and it had little connection to the Mission Management Team, which the Board calls "the single most compelling reason why communications were so poor" [V] (Ch 7, p. 180).
- *Importance of communication.* "At every juncture of STS-107, the Shuttle Program's structure and processes, and therefore the managers in charge, resisted new information." [V] (Ch 7, p. 181). Every manager knew the party line, to wait for the analysis with no safety-of-flight issue expected [AP]; "Program leaders spent at least as much time making sure hierarchical rules and processes were followed as they did trying to establish why anyone would want a picture of the Orbiter." [V] (Ch 7, p. 181).
- *Avoiding oversimplification.* "Over the course of 22 years, foam strikes were normalized to the point where they were simply a "maintenance" issue" [V]. The Challenger legacy biased leaders toward strong signals from the main engines and boosters, while foam strikes were a weak and overlooked signal that proved no less dangerous [AP] (Ch 7, p. 181).
- *Conditioned by success.* Quoting an outside description, the Board says the programme came to remember its brushes with failure as successes [BT]. Managers failed to develop simple contingency plans for a re-entry emergency: "They were convinced, without study, that nothing could be done about such an emergency. The intellectual curiosity and skepticism that a solid safety culture requires was almost entirely absent." [V] "Bureaucracy and process trumped thoroughness and reason." [V] (Ch 7, p. 181).
- *Significance of redundancy.* Workforce reductions and outsourcing culled layers of experience; the move from "oversight" to "insight", aligned with ISO 9000/9001, cut mandatory inspection points by more than half [AP] (Ch 7, p. 181).

From the theories the Board takes two lessons: High Reliability Theory describes the culture NASA should have, including a willingness to learn from mistakes and training that tells employees when to centralise or decentralise; and Normal Accident Theory warns that "Organizations cannot put blind faith into redundant warning systems because they inherently create more complexity" [V] and that people "can, when confronted with extraordinary demands, act in counterproductive ways" [V] (Ch 7, p. 181). Of three alternatives (procedural reform, grounding the Shuttle, structural change), the Board judges structural change the most likely to succeed [AR] (Ch 7, p. 182).

**Best safety practices (Sec 7.3).** The Board compares NASA with the Navy's submarine safety (SUBSAFE) and Naval Reactors programmes and the Aerospace Corporation's launch verification [AE] (Ch 7, pp. 182–184). Naval Reactors has operated for more than 5,500 reactor-years without a reactor accident; its success rests on redundant communication paths, insistence on airing minority opinions, formal written reports, facing facts objectively and managing obsolescence (Ch 7, pp. 182–183). "Unlike NASA, PowerPoint briefings and papers for technical seminars are not substitutes for completed staff work." [V] (Ch 7, p. 182). Naval Reactors has trained more than 5,000 people on the lessons of Challenger [AE] (Ch 7, p. 183). On dissent: "Leaders continually emphasize that when no minority opinions are present, the responsibility for a thorough and critical examination falls to management." [V] "In practice, NASA does not appear to embrace these attitudes." [V] (Ch 7, p. 183). Board interviews found it hard for dissent to percolate up through NASA's hierarchy, despite the anonymous NASA Safety Reporting System [AP] (Ch 7, p. 183). Naval Reactors documents the rationale for every technical requirement and rotates headquarters staff through the field; SUBSAFE allows little tailoring of requirements, verifies compliance through a separate organisation, is relatively immune to budget pressure, and trains on its own past accidents, which NASA does not [AE] (Ch 7, pp. 183–184). At NASA, the programme's control of both engineering and safety compromises the independence of the flight preparation process [AP] (Ch 7, p. 183). The central lesson is the separation of authority between programme managers, "who, by nature, must be sensitive to costs and schedules", and owners of technical requirements and waivers, "who, by nature, are more sensitive to safety and technical rigor" [V] (Ch 7, p. 184). The Aerospace Corporation independently verifies every Air Force launch and is subject to no schedule or cost pressure; its involvement is credited with a 2.9 percent failure rate against 14.6 percent commercially [AE] (Ch 7, p. 184). The section concludes that "responsibility and authority for decisions involving technical requirements and safety should rest with an independent technical authority" [V] (Ch 7, p. 184).

**A broken safety culture (Sec 7.4).** "How could NASA have missed the signals the foam was sending?" [V] was, the Board says, its most perplexing question (Ch 7, p. 184). NASA managers told the Board there was no safety-of-flight issue and that nothing could have been done anyway [AE]; the investigation found "a troubling pattern in which Shuttle Program management made erroneous assumptions about the robustness of a system based on prior success rather than on dependable engineering data and rigorous testing" [V] (Ch 7, p. 184). Safety culture is defined as an organisation's characteristics and attitudes, promoted by its leaders and internalised by its members, that make safety the top priority [AP] (Ch 7, p. 185). The Board's verdict: "the mistakes that were made on STS-107 are not isolated failures, but are indicative of systemic flaws that existed prior to the accident" [V] (Ch 7, p. 185).

The safety organisation's structure is examined in detail [AE] (Ch 7, pp. 185–187). At Kennedy, safety and mission assurance had been placed under the Shuttle Processing Directorate, making it more dependent on the programme. At Johnson, a single Space Shuttle Division Chief represented the Center, the programme and headquarters safety at critical junctures: "It is a single point of failure without any checks or balances." [V] (Ch 7, p. 186). "The Board believes that although the Space Shuttle Program has effective safety practices at the "shop floor" level, its operational and systems safety program is flawed by its dependence on the Shuttle Program." [V] (Ch 7, p. 186). The Shuttle Program Manager had a one-person safety staff, and programmes bought safety services from the Centers, a practice in which "programs sustain the very livelihoods of the safety experts hired to oversee them" [V] (Ch 7, p. 186). The pre-launch safety review asked one division chief to assess his own activities [AE] (Ch 7, p. 187). "Structure and process places Shuttle safety programs in the unenviable position of having to choose between rubber-stamping engineering analyses, technical efforts, and Shuttle program decisions, or trying to carry the day during a committee meeting in which the other side almost always has more information and analytic capability." [V] (Ch 7, p. 187).

On communication, the Board argues that frequent reorganisations created "conditions more conducive to the development of a conventional bureaucracy than to the maintenance of a safety-conscious research-and-development organization" [V], and that "a pattern of ineffective communication has resulted, leaving risks improperly defined, problems unreported, and concerns unexpressed" [V] (Ch 7, p. 187). It treats the communication deficiencies, including those the Shuttle Independent Assessment Team had listed, as a foundation for the accident [AP] (Ch 7, p. 187). Integration was weak: the Orbiter Office was ranked above the Integration Office and did not take part in its board, and "no one office or person in Program management is responsible for developing an integrated risk assessment above the sub-system level" [V] (Ch 7, p. 188). Since 2001 Boeing had done hazard analysis only at the sub-system level, and the bottom-up failure-mode process could not support the top-down analysis managers needed [AE] (Ch 7, p. 188). The Critical Items List held 5,396 hazards, 4,222 of them Criticality 1/1R, with 3,233 waivers, more than 36 percent unreviewed in ten years; the debris hazard report was "ineffectual as a decision aid" [AE] (Ch 7, pp. 188–189). Hazard reports leaned on subjective judgements such as "believed" and "based on experience from previous flights" [AE] (Ch 7, p. 189). A sidebar on cancelled safety upgrades concludes: "Funding a safety upgrade in order to fly safely, and then canceling it for budgetary reasons, makes the concept of mission safety rather hollow." [V] (Ch 7, p. 188). Only foam strikes declared In-Flight Anomalies were entered in the problem-reporting database, which "masks the full extent of the foam debris trends" [V] (Ch 7, p. 189). The section's conclusion: "the Shuttle Program does not use data-driven safety methodologies to their fullest advantage" [V] (Ch 7, p. 189).

**Impact on STS-107 (Sec 7.5).** On programme shortcomings: "Generally, the higher information is transmitted in a hierarchy, the more it gets "rolled-up," abbreviated, and simplified." [V] Weak signals drop out of memos, problem systems and presentations, and "The same conclusions, repeated over time, can result in problems eventually being deemed non-problems." [V] (Ch 7, p. 190). The failure to mention STS-112's foam loss at the STS-107 Flight Readiness Review "desensitized the Shuttle Program to the dangers of foam striking the Thermal Protection System, and demonstrated just how easily the flight preparation process can be compromised" [V] (Ch 7, p. 190). The chair's later admission that the rationale had been poor shows the rationale had been rubber-stamped, which the Board finds unsettling [AP] (Ch 7, p. 190). External pressures shape even data collection and trend analysis, contradicting NASA's belief that pre-flight reviews are true safeguards [AP] (Ch 7, pp. 190–191). "The premium placed on maintaining an operational schedule, combined with ever-decreasing resources, gradually led Shuttle managers and engineers to miss signals of potential danger." [V] (Ch 7, p. 190).

On the Debris Assessment Team, the Board restates the inverted burden of proof: "Organizations that deal with high-risk operations must always have a healthy fear of failure — operations must be proved safe, rather than the other way around. NASA inverted this burden of proof." [V] (Ch 7, p. 190). The Crater work had just moved from Huntington Beach to Houston, a move NASA's own October 2002 risk assessment had predicted would raise risk, and STS-107 was the first mission analysed without Huntington Beach oversight; nobody sought help from the experienced engineers there [AE] (Ch 7, pp. 190–192).

A sidebar, "Engineering by Viewgraphs", examines the slide the Debris Assessment Team used [AE] (Ch 7, p. 191). Its analysis of the slide comes from Edward Tufte and is paraphrased here: the key fact that the projectile was hundreds of times larger than the test data appeared only at the bottom, the title spoke of conservatism, and vague words like "significant" carried several meanings [BT] (Ch 7, p. 191). The Board's own conclusions are its: "As information gets passed up an organization hierarchy, from people who do analysis to mid-level managers to high-level leadership, key explanations and supporting information is filtered out." [V] (Ch 7, p. 191). "The Board views the endemic use of PowerPoint briefing slides instead of technical papers as an illustration of the problematic methods of technical communication at NASA." [V] (Ch 7, p. 191).

On the Mission Management Team, flying STS-113 without a compelling explanation and holding so few meetings "indicates that the Shuttle Program had become overconfident" [V] (Ch 7, p. 192). "All voices must be heard, which can be difficult when facing a hierarchy. An employee's location in the hierarchy can encourage silence." [V] "Organizations interested in safety must take steps to guarantee that all relevant information is presented to decision-makers." [V] (Ch 7, p. 192). The Johnson and Langley engineers kept their concerns in local channels: "They were separated from the decision-making process by distance and rank." [V] (Ch 7, p. 192). Mission Management Team participants felt pressured to stay quiet unless their own area came up, a 40-minute briefing was cut to a three-minute discussion item, and tapes show the leader rushing to a preconceived bottom line [AE] (Ch 7, p. 192). "Organizations with strong safety cultures generally acknowledge that a leader's best response to unanimous consent is to play devil's advocate and encourage an exhaustive debate." [V] "Mission Management Team leaders failed to seek out such minority opinions." [V] "Imagine the difference if any Shuttle manager had simply asked, "Prove to me that Columbia has not been harmed."" [V] (Ch 7, p. 192). Hazard reports, suggestion programmes and time-outs bring minority views forward only if they reduce the fear of retribution and management pays attention; at NASA, "Shuttle Program hazard reporting is seldom used, safety time outs are at times disregarded, and informal efforts to gain support are squelched." [V] (Ch 7, p. 192). On safety: the safety representatives were largely silent, and "That silence was not merely a failure of safety, but a failure of the entire organization." [V] (Ch 7, p. 192).

**Findings and recommendations (Sec 7.6).** The programme combined authority over schedule, cost, manifest, safety, technical requirements and waivers, which the Board judges no effective check and balance [AP] (Ch 7, p. 192). Among the findings: "Over the last two decades, little to no progress has been made toward attaining integrated, independent, and detailed analyses of risk to the Space Shuttle system." [V] (Ch 7, p. 193). Others record that safety organisations depend on the programme for funding, that system safety is separated from mainstream engineering, that the Integration Office is not a true integration office, that integration of responses to bipod shedding did not occur, that the databases are marginally effective, and that NASA has no constructive programme to use past lessons to educate its people [AE] (Ch 7, p. 193). Recommendation R7.5-1 establishes an independent Technical Engineering Authority, funded directly from headquarters with no connection to schedule or cost, which at a minimum develops technical standards, is the sole waiver-granting authority, conducts trend, risk and integrated hazard analysis, owns the failure-mode and hazard-reporting systems, decides what is and is not an anomalous event, and independently verifies launch readiness; R7.5-2 gives the headquarters safety office direct line authority and independent resources; R7.5-3 reorganises the Integration Office to cover every element, the Orbiter included [AP] (Ch 7, p. 193).

### History as cause: Columbia and Challenger (Ch 8)

Chapter 8 compares the two accidents. Its framing questions mirror those of the Rogers Commission: why NASA kept flying with a known problem, and why managers concluded the problem was not a threat despite their engineers' concerns [AP] (Ch 8, p. 195). Board member Sally Ride, who also sat on the Rogers Commission, heard "echoes" of Challenger in Columbia [AE] (Ch 8, p. 195). "The foam debris hit was not the single cause of the Columbia accident, just as the failure of the joint seal that permitted O-ring erosion was not the single cause of Challenger." [V] (Ch 8, p. 195). The explanation is about system effects, how decisions in one layer of NASA's organisational system (the political and budgetary layer of Chapter 5) shaped another (the culture and safety structure of Chapter 7) and so the decisions of Chapter 6 [AR] (Ch 8, p. 195). "Each is a critical link in the causal chain." [V] (Ch 8, p. 195). Both accidents were failures of foresight, a term the Board takes from Barry Turner's study of man-made disasters [BT] (Ch 8, p. 195).

The Board draws three conclusions [AR] (Ch 8, p. 195): the causes of the institutional failure behind Challenger have not been fixed; "if these persistent, systemic flaws are not resolved, the scene is set for another accident" [V]; and its focus on context does not excuse individuals (Ch 8, p. 195). The White House and Congress must recognise their part and take responsibility for safety in future [AP] (Ch 8, p. 196).

**Failures of foresight and the normalisation of deviance (Sec 8.2).** The Board tried to see the foam incidents as NASA engineers and managers saw them at the time, rather than in hindsight [AP] (Ch 8, p. 196). "In both cases, engineers and managers conducting risk assessments continually normalized the technical deviations they found." [V] Evidence that the design was not performing as expected "was reinterpreted as acceptable and non-deviant, which diminished perceptions of risk throughout the agency" [V] (Ch 8, p. 196).
