The mechanism is stated precisely [AR] (Ch 8, p. 196). Neither O-ring erosion nor foam debris was predicted by the original design, and the first occurrence of each was a violation of specification. In both cases the first engineering analysis concluded the design could tolerate the damage, and a temporary fix or acceptance of risk followed. "For both O-rings and foam, that first decision was a turning point. It established a precedent for accepting, rather than eliminating, these technical deviations." [V] Subsequent incidents were read "as evidence that the design was now acting as predicted" [V], and the engineering experience base "functioned as an elastic waistband, expanding to hold larger deviations from the original design" [V]. "Anomalies that did not lead to catastrophic failure were treated as a source of valid engineering data that justified further flights." [V] "Engineers understood what was happening, but they never understood why." [V] (Ch 8, p. 196).

Official classifications were downgraded over time: foam events lost In-Flight Anomaly status, and STS-112's was downgraded to an action; the booster joint went from Criticality 1 to 1R and was closed out of the problem system the month before Challenger [AE] (Ch 8, pp. 196–197). Tile damage had been budgeted as maintenance from the start, so foam damage slotted into an existing category, and foam events came to be called "in-family": "a strange term indeed for a violation of system requirements" [V] (Ch 8, p. 196). Three features made the signals hard to read [AR] (Ch 8, pp. 196–197). The Shuttle was an experimental vehicle on which many anomalies were expected, so an anomaly was not in itself a warning. Incidents were examined one at a time. And a danger signal was followed by flights where the machine behaved, so managers received mixed signals. Strong signals, such as wiring faults or cracked strut assemblies with a clear link to loss of mission, did stop launches; foam and O-ring erosion were defined as nagging issues of little consequence (Ch 8, p. 197).

"History became cause as the repeating pattern of anomalies was ratified as safe in Flight Readiness Reviews." [V] (Ch 8, p. 197). Both accidents had a surprise that could have been a wake-up call: blackened putty after a cold January 1985 launch, and STS-112's large foam strike in October 2002 [AE] (Ch 8, p. 197). In both, the strong signal was redefined as weak after analysis: "After analysis, the biggest foam hit to date was redefined as a weak signal." [V] (Ch 8, p. 197). The Board rejects the hindsight framing of Feynman's Russian-roulette comparison, which it paraphrases [BT]: "But that characterization is only possible in hindsight." [V] Fixes were in hand for both problems but neither was defined as a show-stopper, and "Taken one at a time, each decision seemed correct." [V] (Ch 8, p. 197).

**System effects (Sec 8.3).** "NASA remained a politicized and vulnerable agency, dependent on key political players who accepted NASA's ambitious proposals and then imposed strict budget limits." [V] (Ch 8, p. 197). Culture, structure and the safety system combined to keep NASA on a "slippery slope": a culture that allowed flying with flaws defined as normal, a structure that blocked the flow of critical information up the hierarchy, and a weakened safety system that could only ratify existing risk assessments [AP] (Ch 8, p. 197). "The harmful effects of schedule pressure identified in previous reports had returned." [V] (Ch 8, p. 198). "NASA was cutting corners." [V] (Ch 8, p. 198). "The NASA culture encouraged flying with flaws because the schedule could not be held up for routine problems that were not defined as a threat to mission safety." [V] (Ch 8, p. 198). Post-Challenger structural changes "were undone over time by management actions" [V] (Ch 8, p. 198). The Flight Readiness process, "which is built on consensus verified by signatures of all responsible parties, in effect renders no one accountable" [V]; information was lost at each level because of the need for brevity and consensus; and the process "was designed to assess hardware and take corrective actions that would transform known problems into acceptable flight risks, and that is precisely what it did" [V] (Ch 8, p. 198). As for safety, "when pressed for cost reduction, NASA attacked its own safety system" [V] (Ch 8, p. 199). "Post-Challenger NASA still had no systematic procedure for identifying and monitoring trends." [V] (Ch 8, p. 199). In one case a single person held at least three safety positions [AE] (Ch 8, p. 199).

**Organisation, culture and unintended consequences (Sec 8.4).** "Streamlining and downsizing, which scarcely go unnoticed by employees, convey a message that efficiency is an important goal." [V] With evening and weekend work for Node 2, "faster, better, cheaper" and cuts to safety staff, "efficiency becomes a strong signal and safety a weak one" [V] (Ch 8, p. 199). The Rogers Commission had found NASA blinded by its can-do attitude, and the Board found the same belief in an operational system and the same reluctance to listen to outside experts [BT] (Ch 8, p. 199). "Can-Do", taken too far, "can create a reluctance to say that something cannot be done" [V] (Ch 8, p. 199). "How could the lessons of Challenger have been forgotten so quickly?" [V] (Ch 8, p. 199). Seventeen years and 87 missions without major incident made the machine look successful, and the Apollo-era deference to working engineers' expertise had been overridden by an allegiance to hierarchy, procedure and chain of command, a pattern the Board names with a term from the organisational literature, bureaucratic accountability [BT] (Ch 8, p. 199). The layers of process, boards and panels that had given false confidence before Challenger returned in full before Columbia, and the many post-Challenger changes themselves supported a belief that the system was safe [AP] (Ch 8, p. 199).

**Two decision sequences compared (Sec 8.5).** Challenger's decision was a single pre-launch teleconference among 34 people in three places, which reverted, without ground rules, to the hierarchical model of the Flight Readiness Review; Columbia's was spread over days after launch [AE] (Ch 8, pp. 199–200). For Columbia, engineers at four Centers "showed initiative and jumped on the problem without direction from above" [V], forming working groups and e-mail groups spontaneously; this showed "that NASA's original technical culture was alive and well" [V], but the diffuse form of the rest of the proceedings had negative consequences (Ch 8, p. 200). "In both situations, all new information was weighed and interpreted against past experience." [V] "Pre-existing definitions of risk shaped the actions taken and not taken." [V] (Ch 8, p. 200). Worried engineers in both years "could not prove that foam strikes and cold temperatures were unsafe, even though the previous analyses that declared them safe had been incomplete and were based on insufficient data and testing" [V] (Ch 8, p. 200). "The obstacles these engineers faced were political and organizational." [V] (Ch 8, p. 200).

The section's systemic statements, printed in italics in the report, are each followed by their effect on decisions [AR] (Ch 8, pp. 200–202):

- *Conflicting goals.* "NASA's conflicting goals put engineers at a disadvantage before these new situations even arose." [V] (Ch 8, p. 200). In both cases, "managers' techniques focused on the information that tended to support the expected or desired result at that time" [V] and drew conclusions that minimised the risk of delay (Ch 8, p. 200). The Mission Management Team chair's dual role as launch integration manager for the next flight was, in the Board's words, "a dual role promoting a conflict of interest and a single-point failure" [V] (Ch 8, p. 200). "NASA had conflicting goals of cost, schedule, and safety. Safety lost out as the mandates of an "operational system" increased the schedule pressure." [V] (Ch 8, p. 200).
- *Bureaucratic accountability.* "NASA's culture of bureaucratic accountability emphasized chain of command, procedure, following the rules, and going by the book." [V] Allegiance to hierarchy and procedure had replaced deference to engineers' technical expertise [AP] (Ch 8, p. 200). In both cases engineers brought concerns and solutions (a request for images; a temperature constraint on launch), and "Management did not listen to what their engineers were telling them. Instead, rules and procedures took priority." [V] (Ch 8, p. 201). The Debris Assessment Team was asked to demonstrate a "mandatory need" for imagery "but were not told how to do that" [V], and both teams faced a reversed standard: "instead of having to prove it was safe to fly, they were asked to prove that it was unsafe to fly" [V] (Ch 8, p. 201). Managers held engineers to protocol while their own meetings ran loose and irregular, letting informal influence and status shape decisions [AP] (Ch 8, p. 201). "In highly uncertain circumstances, when lives were immediately at risk, management failed to defer to its engineers and failed to recognize that different data standards — qualitative, subjective, and intuitive — and different processes — democratic rather than protocol and chain of command — were more appropriate." [V] (Ch 8, p. 201).
- *Structure and hierarchy.* "The organizational structure and hierarchy blocked effective communication of technical problems. Signals were overlooked, people were silenced, and useful information and dissenting views on technical issues did not surface at higher levels." [V] "Structure and hierarchy represent power and status." [V] For both accidents, "employees' positions in the organization determined the weight given to their information, by their own judgment and in the eyes of others" [V] (Ch 8, p. 201). At the Challenger teleconference some engineers did not think themselves qualified to speak; the contractor's managers caucused off-line and made a management decision in which "Managers voted and engineers did not." [V] (Ch 8, p. 201); when asked whether anyone had anything to add, no one spoke [AE]. For Columbia, the Kennedy imagery request came from a "low status" Center; the Debris Assessment Team worked at the margins of the hierarchy; a demoralised team dropped its imagery slide; and uncertainties fell out when a formal presentation was condensed to a verbal brief [AE] (Ch 8, p. 201). In the informal chain of command, "location in the structure empowered some to speak and silenced others" [V] (Ch 8, p. 201); a tile expert with an office in the Shuttle Program used his network to shape the Mission Management Team's view and snuff out dissent [AP] (Ch 8, p. 201). "Status mattered. In its absence, numbers were the great equalizer." [V] The tile expert's word was taken as gospel though he lacked RCC expertise, data or analysis, while those of lesser standing faced a stringent and inhibiting requirement for data [AP] (Ch 8, p. 202). The Debris Assessment Team's members, like the Thiokol engineers, did not speak when asked, intimidated by the chair's position and the conclusions she had already reached; they signed off on Crater results they found hard to understand, and still wanted images [AE] (Ch 8, p. 202).
- *Dependence on contractors.* NASA accepted both contractors' risk assessments though each was full of uncertainty: Thiokol's managers reversed their engineers' recommendation after a senior vice-president urged a management view, and NASA accepted Boeing's use of Crater 400 times outside its validated limits [AE] (Ch 8, p. 202).
- *A silent safety system.* No safety representative was at the Challenger teleconference; at Columbia's meetings, "rather than critically question or actively participate in the analysis, the safety representatives simply listened and concurred" [V] (Ch 8, p. 202).

The comparison ends: "In neither impending crisis did management recognize how structure and hierarchy can silence employees and follow through by polling participants, soliciting dissenting opinions, or bringing in outsiders who might have a different perspective or useful information." [V] Both crews were told there was no problem [AE] (Ch 8, p. 202).

**Changing NASA's organisational system (Sec 8.6).** The flawed practices persisted for 20 years and contributed to both accidents, and the Board judges that NASA has shown little understanding of how its own organisation works [AP] (Ch 8, p. 202). NASA managers believed they had a strong safety culture, but responses to the imagery requests and to engineers' speculative e-mails showed otherwise [AP] (Ch 8, p. 202). "The Board found that Mission Management Team decision-making operated outside the rules even as it held its engineers to a stifling protocol." [V] "Management was not able to recognize that in unprecedented conditions, when lives are on the line, flexibility and democratic process should take priority over bureaucratic response." [V] (Ch 8, p. 203).

The Board sets out principles to govern change [AR] (Ch 8, p. 203):

- *Leaders create culture.* "Leaders create culture. It is their responsibility to change it." [V] "Leaders are responsible for establishing the conditions that lead to their subordinates' successes or failures." [V] National leaders set the accident in motion by creating resource and schedule strains [AP]. "But the Space Shuttle is not now, nor has it ever been, an operational vehicle. We cannot explore space on a fixed-cost basis." [V] "National leadership needs to recognize that NASA must fly only when it is ready." [V] (Ch 8, p. 203).
- *Strengthen signals.* "Strategies must increase the clarity, strength, and presence of signals that challenge assumptions about risk." [V] Twice in its history NASA went down a slippery slope to catastrophe: "Each decision, taken by itself, seemed correct, routine, and indeed, insignificant and unremarkable. Yet in retrospect, the cumulative effect was stunning." [V] Events "unfolded over a long time and in small increments rather than in sudden and dramatic occurrences" [V]. "NASA's challenge is to design systems that maximize the clarity of signals, amplify weak signals so they can be tracked, and account for missing signals." [V] The missing signals were the lack of trend analysis, imagery not obtained, concerns not voiced, and information overlooked or dropped from briefings [AP]. "A safety team must have equal and independent representation so that managers are not again lulled into complacency by shifting definitions of risk." [V] (Ch 8, p. 203).
- *The marginal voice.* "It is obvious but worth acknowledging that people who are marginal and powerless in organizations may have useful information or opinions that they don't express. Even when these people are encouraged to speak, they find it intimidating to contradict a leader's strategy or a group consensus." [V] "Extra effort must be made to contribute all relevant information to discussions of risk." [V] "Because ill-structured problems are less visible and therefore invite the normalization of deviance, they may be the most risky of all." [V] (Ch 8, p. 203).
- *Change structure with care.* "Changes in organizational structure should be made only with careful consideration of their effect on the system and their possible unintended consequences. Changes that make the organization more complex may create new ways that it can fail." [V] Change initially raises the risk of error and loses institutional memory, and is complicated by politics, leaders' limited view of consequences, insiders' interests and the failure to learn from the past [AP]. Nonetheless changes must be made: "NASA's blind spot is it believes it has a strong safety culture." [V] The structure must be changed to restore deference to technical experts, empower engineers to get resources, and let safety concerns be freely aired [AP] (Ch 8, p. 203).

The chapter's endnotes draw on the organisational literature (Turner, Vaughan, Starbuck and Milliken, McCurdy, Weick's advice that people learn to recognise unprecedented situations in which following the rules can be disastrous, and work on how organisations backslide once a crisis ebbs) [BT] (Ch 8, p. 204).

## Part IV: A look ahead (Part Three, Ch 9–11)

### Implications for the future of human space flight (Ch 9)

The chapter is divided into near term (return to flight), mid term (continuing to fly the Shuttle) and long term (future directions) [AP] (Ch 9, p. 207). It begins with a caution: "In this report we have documented numerous indications that NASA's safety performance has been lacking. But even correcting all those shortcomings, it should be understood, will not eliminate risk." [V] (Ch 9, p. 207). Risk concentrates at the start and end of a flight; Challenger was lost just over a minute after launch and Columbia about 16 minutes before landing [AE] (Ch 9, p. 207). Human space flight "must be viewed as a developmental activity. It is still far from a routine, operational undertaking." [V] (Ch 9, p. 208). The Shuttle is not comparable to air transport, and if its operations came to look routine it was because of the skill of the people involved: "They have made it look easy, though in fact it never was." [V] (Ch 9, p. 208).

**Near term.** "The recognition of human spaceflight as a developmental activity requires a shift in focus from operations and meeting schedules to a concern for the risks involved." [V] (Ch 9, p. 208). The necessary measures begin with "Identifying risks by looking relentlessly for the next eroding O-ring, the next falling foam; obtaining better data, analyzing and spotting trends." [V], and continue with stopping failures at their source, decoupling unforeseen events from loss of crew and vehicle, exploring every option for survival, and barring unwarranted departures from design standards [AP] (Ch 9, p. 208).

**Mid term.** The Board's view is that "the present Shuttle is not inherently unsafe" [V], provided the report's recommendations are carried out, including all Part One recommendations, all Part Two organisational and cultural changes, and recertification (Ch 9, p. 208). The urgency comes from a predictable decay: "That energy will inevitably dissipate over time. This decline in vigilance is a characteristic of many large organizations, and it has been demonstrated in NASA's own history." [V] (Ch 9, p. 208). The organisational changes are separating technical authority from schedule and cost, an independent safety organisation and effective systems integration; the cultural changes are harder, and "cultural problems are unlikely to be corrected without top-level leadership" [V] (Ch 9, p. 208). That leadership must rid the system of practices kept only because they are old: keeping knowledge of problems within a Center or programme, making technical decisions without peer-reviewed analysis, and an unofficial hierarchy or caste system created by concentrating power in one office [AP] (Ch 9, p. 208). Recommendation R9.1-1, a return-to-flight item, requires a detailed plan for the independent Technical Engineering Authority, the independent safety programme and the reorganised Integration Office, with annual reports to Congress; enforcement rests with the White House and Congress [AP] (Ch 9, pp. 208–209). R9.2-1 requires recertification of the vehicle at every level before operating it beyond 2010; the Shuttle lacks the closed-loop feedback that aviation uses to manage ageing [AP] (Ch 9, p. 209).

**Long term.** NASA has had no compelling national mandate for human space flight since Apollo, has had to court diverse constituencies, and has usually been funded below its ambitions, leaving it straining to do too much with too little [AP] (Ch 9, p. 209). Attempts to replace the Shuttle failed because they depended on technological breakthroughs [AP] (Ch 9, pp. 209–211). The Board concludes that the Shuttle should be replaced as soon as possible as the primary means of carrying people to orbit, that the replacement's design should give overriding priority to crew safety rather than trading safety against cost or other capabilities, and that "One of the major problems with the way the Space Shuttle Program was carried out was an a priori fixed ceiling on development costs. That approach should not be repeated." [V] (Ch 9, p. 211). Previous attempts to develop a replacement "represent a failure of national leadership" [AP] (Ch 9, p. 211).

### Other significant observations (Ch 10)

Chapter 10 collects issues found during the investigation that did not cause the accident but fall, in the Board's words, into the category of "weak signals" of possible future problems [AP] (Ch 10, p. 213).

- *Public safety (Sec 10.1).* A Board-commissioned study found the absence of ground casualties was the expected outcome, though there was a 9 to 24 percent chance of at least one serious injury; NASA had made no documented effort to assess public risk from re-entry, and the Board holds that NASA should be legally responsible for public safety in every phase of flight [AE] (Ch 10, pp. 213–214).
- *Crew escape and survival (Sec 10.2).* Columbia broke up in a phase that offered no possibility of crew survival under the current design [AE] (Ch 10, p. 214). Before Challenger, "NASA believed if the Orbiter could be saved, then the crew would be safe" [V] (Ch 10, p. 215). The Board's principle: "The sole objective must be the highest probability of a crew's safe return" [V] (Ch 10, p. 216). "Space flight is an inherently dangerous undertaking, and will remain so for the foreseeable future." [V] (Ch 10, p. 217).
- *Engineering drawings and closeout photos (Sec 10.3).* The drawing system is paper-based, inaccurate and slow (up to four weeks to obtain drawings, six for closeout photos), and inadequate for another 20 years' use [AE] (Ch 10, p. 217).
- *Industrial safety and quality assurance (Sec 10.4).* Industrial safety was healthy, with programmes that let any employee call a time-out [AE] (Ch 10, pp. 217–218). Quality assurance was not: Kennedy had cut government inspection points by more than 80 percent; a request for a main-engine final review had been denied for two years for lack of staff; inspection changes were constrained by "institutional dogma that the status quo is based on strong engineering logic" [V] (Ch 10, p. 218). Kennedy no longer closed the loop on discrepancies, components marked "ground test only" had flown, and of 141,127 inspections only 20 rejections were recorded, a statistically improbable rate that technicians confirmed was not credible [AE] (Ch 10, p. 219).
- *Maintenance documentation, Orbiter maintenance periods and corrosion (Sec 10.5–10.7).* Paperwork errors recurred in categories reviewers did not know to look for; modification work had grown from 20 planned items to 84 on one Orbiter, and "Such changes introduce turmoil and increase the potential for mistakes." [V] (Ch 10, p. 221). A proposal to lengthen maintenance intervals ran counter to the industry norm of inspecting ageing systems more often [AP] (Ch 10, p. 221). About 10 percent of the Orbiter's structure cannot be inspected for corrosion [AE] (Ch 10, p. 221).
- *Bolts, hold-down posts and the attach ring (Sec 10.8–10.10).* The Board records brittle fractures in wing bolts, an intermittent failure of the hold-down post firing system on STS-112 that pre-launch testing might not catch, and the attach-ring safety factor reduced from 1.4 to 1.25 to accommodate the launch schedule after only a cursory briefing [AE] (Ch 10, pp. 222–223). NASA's reliance on "analysis" rather than test is, the Board says, endemic [AP] (Ch 10, p. 223).
- *Test equipment and leadership training (Sec 10.11–10.12).* Technicians still used 1970s analogue equipment; and NASA managers up to Associate Administrator had taken their posts without a standard programme of management and leadership training, unlike the military [AE] (Ch 10, p. 223).

### Recommendations (Ch 11)

The chapter lists all the report's recommendations by subject, return-to-flight items first, in no order of priority [AP] (Ch 11, p. 225). It opens with the view that good leadership can direct a culture to adapt to new realities, and: "NASA's culture must change, and the Board intends the following recommendations to be steps toward effecting this change." [V] (Ch 11, p. 225). Part One recommendations cover the Thermal Protection System, imaging, sensor data, wiring, bolt catchers, closeouts, micrometeoroid and orbital debris, and foreign-object debris; Part Two's cover scheduling (R6.2-1), Mission Management Team training (R6.3-1) and organisation (R7.5-1 to 7.5-3); Part Three's cover the implementation plan (R9.1-1), recertification (R9.2-1), and closeout photographs and drawings (R10.3-1, R10.3-2) [AE] (Ch 11, pp. 225–227).

## Part V: The investigation (Appendices A–C)

Appendix A describes how the Board worked, and is the report's account of its own method [AE] (App A, pp. 231–238). The Board was activated at 10:30 a.m. on 1 February under NASA's post-Challenger contingency plan, with seven members holding designated government posts; Admiral Harold Gehman was named chair, and the Board renamed itself and rewrote its charter in its first week to secure its independence: its own staff, budget and records, the chair's power to appoint members, public updates, simultaneous release of its report to all parties, and the right of members to write minority reports (App A, pp. 231–232). With five additional members it reached 13, the same as the Rogers Commission; it worked in four groups (materials and management; training and operations; engineering and technical analysis; history, budget and culture) with an Independent Assessment Team to check NASA's analysis (App A, p. 232).

The Board chose to run a safety investigation rather than one to assign blame. "Rather than assign formal blame or determine legal liability for the cause of the accident, the Board affirmed its charge to pursue both an accident investigation and a safety investigation, the primary aim of which would be to identify and correct threats to the safe operation of the Space Shuttle." [V] (App A, p. 232). To that end it took privileged witness statements. Safety investigations "place a premium on obtaining full and complete disclosure about every aspect of an accident, even if that information may prove damaging or embarrassing to particular individuals or organizations" [V] (App A, p. 232). People who have made mistakes or know of others' negligence often fear being fired or prosecuted if they speak, and confidentiality lets them volunteer information and speculate about their organisations' flaws more openly than they would in public [AP] (App A, pp. 232–233). Statements were not under oath, were transcribed and signed by the witness, were restricted to the 13 members and a few staff, and were exempt from disclosure [AE] (App A, p. 233). Accountability was not abandoned, only separated: "The existence of a safety investigation in which privileged statements are taken does not prevent an accounting of personal responsibility associated with an accident. It merely means that such an accounting must result from a separate investigation." [V] (App A, p. 233). That accounting was left to NASA and Congress, and the Board pledged to report any evidence of criminal activity or willful negligence [AE] (App A, p. 233).

Other procedures [AE] (App A, pp. 233–236): the scope was expanded, at Congress's request, to the whole history of the Shuttle Program; investigators were authorised in writing; the Board kept to the standards of openness of the Federal Advisory Committee Act though not bound by it; its members were made federal employees; the NASA Inspector General could attend its proceedings; it had its own budget; more than 750 of some 3,000 public submissions led to action. More than 600 written requests to NASA were signed by Board members, tracked and closed only when the requesting member signed off (App A, p. 234). The chair asked NASA to move the managers involved in STS-107 out of directly managing or supporting the investigation, to avoid actual or perceived conflicts of interest (App A, pp. 234–235). Mission data, hardware and facilities were impounded; Mission Control's door was locked while data was backed up and statements were taken; nothing was released or tested without the chair's approval (App A, p. 235). The Board kept its own databases on a Justice Department server, independent of NASA's, holding more than 450,000 pages (App A, pp. 235–236). Public hearings ran from March to June 2003, one of them on risk assessment in complex organisations with Diane Vaughan as witness (App A, pp. 237–238).

Appendix B gives the members' biographies, and Appendix C lists the staff; among the Group II staff is Diane Vaughan, listed as a researcher, and the consultants include the organisational scholars named in Chapter 7 [AE] (App B, pp. 239–241; App C, pp. 243–248).

## Connections the author makes in the text

- **Rogers Commission (Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident, 1986).** The reference point for the whole of Part Two: its findings on the joint, the silent safety system, schedule pressure and the Flight Readiness process, and its recommendations, many of which the Board finds undone; critical of NASA's follow-through, approving of the Commission [BT] (Ch 1, pp. 24–25; Ch 5, pp. 99–101; Ch 7, p. 178; Ch 8, pp. 195–203).
- **Diane Vaughan, *The Challenger Launch Decision* (1996) and other papers.** The source of the "normalization of deviance" and of the analysis of how risk was redefined before Challenger; Vaughan also appears as a Board staff researcher and hearing witness; approving [BT] (Ch 1, p. 24; Ch 6, p. 130; Ch 8, pp. 196–204; App A, p. 238; App C, p. 244).
- **Richard Feynman's appendix to the Rogers report.** Cited for the Russian-roulette comparison, which the Board says is possible only in hindsight; qualified [BT] (Ch 6, p. 130; Ch 8, p. 197).
- **High Reliability Theory and Normal Accident Theory** (with Karl Weick, Karlene Roberts, Todd La Porte and Paula Consolini, Scott Sagan and Charles Perrow cited in the endnotes). Used as yardsticks, neither entirely appropriate alone; approving with qualification [BT] (Ch 7, pp. 180–182, 194).
- **Barry Turner, *Man-made Disasters*.** Source of the term failures of foresight; approving [BT] (Ch 8, pp. 195, 204).
- **Edward Tufte.** His analysis of the Debris Assessment Team slide; approving [BT] (Ch 7, p. 191).
- **Navy SUBSAFE, Naval Reactors and the Aerospace Corporation.** Benchmarks for independent technical authority and safety; approving [BT] (Ch 7, pp. 182–184).
- **Shuttle Independent Assessment Team (1999), Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel, General Accounting Office (1990), Kraft Report (1995).** Earlier reviews whose warnings went unheeded (or, for the Kraft Report, whose view of a mature Shuttle the Board rejects); approving except the Kraft Report [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 108–114; Ch 7, pp. 178–179).
- **Howard McCurdy, Garry Brewer and other organisational scholars.** Cited on NASA's technical culture and its resistance to criticism; approving [BT] (Ch 5, pp. 101–102; Ch 8, p. 199).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Stopping at the last step or the nearest person.* Investigations that "blame a failure only on the last step" and correct by replacing or retraining people (Board Statement, p. 6; Part Two, p. 97; Ch 7, p. 177).
- *Personnel change as the fix.* NASA's problems "cannot be solved simply by retirements, resignations, or transferring personnel" (Ch 8, p. 195).
- *The Shuttle as "operational".* The vehicle is and always was developmental (Ch 1, p. 25; Ch 8, p. 203; Ch 9, p. 208).
- *Past success as evidence of safety.* Using successful flights as the rationale for the next, without engineering analysis (Ch 6, p. 126; Ch 7, p. 177).
- *Requiring proof of danger.* Asking engineers to prove a situation unsafe instead of requiring it to be proved safe (Ch 6, p. 169; Ch 7, p. 190; Ch 8, p. 201).
- *"Nothing could be done".* The untested assumption that a damaged Orbiter could not be saved (Ch 6, pp. 121, 174; Ch 7, p. 181).
- *Briefing by slide.* PowerPoint in place of technical papers (Ch 7, pp. 182, 191).
- *Hindsight framings.* The Russian-roulette comparison as a description of how risk was perceived at the time (Ch 8, p. 197).
- *Safety bought by the programme it oversees.* Funding and staffing arrangements that make safety dependent on the programme (Ch 7, pp. 186–187).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Conversion.** The PDF (250 pages, 157 MB, SHA-256 `5d92cd1f…4c4586f`) is not in the repository, being over GitHub's file-size limit. The operator converted it with `pdftotext 26.08.0` (default mode; deterministic, no model-mediated extraction) from the PDF's OCR text layer and staged the text, which this run moved from `sources/ingest/` to `sources/converted/caib-report-vol1.md`. The text has 25,038 lines and 166,877 words and contains 250 form feeds, one per PDF page boundary; it runs from the cover to the end of Appendix C, with no truncation marker.

**Citation style.** `(Ch N, p. M)` with printed page numbers. The printed numbers survive in about half the running heads, sometimes garbled ("1 72", "2 qS", "7-02"). On every page where they are legible, the count of form feeds before a line equals the printed page number, so that count was used for every citation in this reference. A helper computed each quotation's page from its line, and a check matched every `[V]` citation's page to the page on which the quotation sits in the converted text.

**OCR damage, and how it was handled.** Body prose is largely clean. Damage concentrates in endnote numbers and markers, tables, figure captions, figures (which survive as scattered fragments), running heads, and the findings and recommendation lists, where F-numbers sometimes separate from their text or are lost (Section 6.3's findings after F6.3-8 lose several numbers; Section 6.3's recommendation R6.3-1 is truncated at line ends in the chapter, though its full text survives in Chapter 11). Scattered words in body prose are also damaged ("en g ineers'", "safetyof-flight", "followthrough", "Cobnnbia", "hi-h-pressure", "hying", "engenderin g", "accountahility", "a u-uly indepen[dent]"). Every passage containing such a word was paraphrased, not quoted. The operator's check found the columns of Chapters 5–8 in reading order, and that holds for nearly all body prose; but on p. 202 (Ch 8) the end of a sentence about contractor dependence ("by NASA's dependence on the contractor") is placed about 80 lines before its start, and on p. 203 the sentence "Twice in NASA history, the agency embarked on a slippery slope" is split across a column boundary, so only the contiguous sentences after it are quoted. Every `[V]` was checked with `scripts/check-verbatim.py` against the converted text and is contiguous there.

**No second OCR.** The protocol asks for the quoted pages of a scanned source to be re-OCR'd with tesseract and the quotations checked against both readings. The PDF is not in this environment, so that check was not run here; it is the first thing Pass I should do, from the operator's local copy.

**Third-party material.** See the header. All `[V]` quotations are the Board's own prose. Chapter 8 draws heavily on Vaughan's framework, and Vaughan served on the Board's staff (App C, p. 244); the chapter's text is nonetheless the Board's report, so its sentences are quoted where clean, while the term "normalization of deviance" and the ideas the chapter credits to Vaughan are marked `[BT]`. Quoted e-mails, log entries, meeting transcripts, testimony and press remarks by individuals (Chapters 2, 6 and 8) are reported in the Board's words. NASA's own definitions and requirement text quoted in the report (the in-family definitions in Ch 6; the human-rating requirements in Ch 10) are paraphrased because they are quoted documents, not the Board's prose. The Boeing-credited figure in Chapter 9 is not described beyond its caption.

**Source inconsistencies, recorded as found.** Chapter 3's impact-test conclusion gives Columbia's liftoff as "January 23, 2003" (p. 83); the launch was 16 January (Ch 2, p. 33). The Flight Day 2 object's decay date is 19 January in Chapter 2 and 20 January in Chapter 3. The caption of the debris-damage chart in Chapter 6 runs "through STS-173", a mission that did not exist (p. 127). The Chapter 6 debris table dates STS-62 to October 1994 while the text gives 4 March 1994 (pp. 124, 128). The text spells the probabilistic tile study's second author "Fishback" while the endnote has "Fischbeck" (pp. 129–130, 176). "Principle metrics" for "principal metrics" (Ch 6, p. 132) and "independant" (Synopsis, p. 12) are the report's spellings. The Challenger launch caption in Chapter 8 gives the mission as "STS-33/51-L" (p. 203).

**Rescue and repair.** Section 6.4 rests on a study NASA performed at the Board's request after the accident; its conclusions are NASA's assessment as the Board reports it.
